Q60.original_text: I have experienced anxiety and depression during my MSc and PhD programs, but not associated with my academic studies. My university has some nice resources that I was able to use during that time, which it promotes regularly among students. I feel that my PI/research group would be relatively open to discussing mental health, but I wish this was a more proactive thing. I think my group could do more to make sure that we all have tools for preventative mental health care. My group functions in a way that puts relatively little stress on us individually in ways that might jeopardize our mental health, but I would prefer to make explicit why this kind of lab culture is important.  I also want to address some of the questions that were about lab culture and expectations in my experience/at my university. While my own experience has been overwhelmingly positive, I know that in other groups in other departments the experience is very different. In this regard, my university does not have a generalized culture, and some people do go through bullying, pressure to work late, etc. There seems to be a lingering sense of tradition, that this is what academia is like. It emphasizes to me again why it is so important to have discussions, to say things, to make things explicit, and to be nonjudging about other people's perspectives. As an example, a senior scientist in my group sometimes leaves early to attend a function at her child's school, and she tells us that is what she is doing. Academia can be this, too.

Q26.text: Honestly? It's a mixed bag. The funding and resources are solid, but the admin processes are painfully slow and the culture can be surprisingly isolated. You have to be self-driven just to get anything done.
Q26.original_text: I have an extremely low opinion of the academic system after my PhD experience. I was excited to work in an environment where creativity and new ideas were appreciated and I could learn new things all the time. I expected that I would work hard and long hours, but not so hard that I burnt myself out. However, looking back now, I absolutely wouldn't do this again, and I wish I had quit during my qualifying exams like I wanted to, but I was talked out of it. Sexual harassment and bullying are so pervasive that at this point I am surprised when my peers haven't experienced it. Expectations are consistently unreasonable and students completely burn themselves out trying to meet them and receive little to no recognition when they do. Stipends are so low that many graduate students struggle to make ends meet, to the point where many experience food insecurity. Professors receive little to no training on management, mentoring, or teaching, which causes harm to students when do all of these jobs poorly. Funding is extremely inequitably distributed, with "big name" labs and a handful of "prestigious" universities getting a huge amount of the funding, and other labs doing valuable work struggle to get a single grant. Also, basic research projects trying to generate new knowledge, which are supposed to be the lifeblood of academia, are almost never funded. To be funded now, research apparently has to have immediately realizable applications.  There is no diversity of thought among faculty, as the only people who can actually become faculty now all come from the same few universities, and in many cases even from the same advisors. People who struggle with their mental health during graduate school are often driven out rather than helped. Teaching loads are often unreasonable and don't even teach valuable skills, but simply take up graduate students' time. Universities use bureaucracy as a way to keep from making changes, and it is easier for them to just wait out student complaints until they graduate rather than address them. Graduate programs are not actually set up for graduate students to learn, as the "degree" would lead you to think - it is set up to use graduate students as a source of cheap labor to generate research and revenue for the university. In turn, the university barely acknowledges graduate students, focusing their energy and resources on undergraduate students and faculty. Diversity is not valued, and people from diverse backgrounds are much more likely to quit at every stage because the environment is untenable for them.

Q26.text: Ate o momento, consigo  perceber que fazer um Doutorado em um pais com uma cultura extremamente diferente e que e automaticamente refletida na cultura educacional, e um desafio tremendo, que tem impacto direto na saude mental dos estudantes. Por exemplo, venho da cultura ocidental, onde hierarquias quase sao nulas (as relacoes sao bem horizontais); a autonomia, a proatividade e a liberdade no ambiente academica sao consideradas como qualidade e bem vistas pelos Professores; o equilibrio entre vida pessoal e profissional tambem sao bem vistos e devem co-existir. Entretanto, no Japao, a sociedade e extremamente hierarquizada e essa hierarquia e refletida fortemente no ambiente academico, onde os professores sao tomam uma posicao enorme de poder e respeito, colocando-os em uma posicao inacessivel ao estudante. E isso abre tambem precedentes gravissimos para a quase institucionalizacao do abuso moral e de poder (e, uma vez, que a hierarquia e sumariamente respeitada, esses episodios quase nao sao reportados por parte dos estudantes). Ainda, considerando esse posicionamento dos professores nessa hierarquia engessada, os estudantes nao sao bem vistos se questionam, apresentam personalidade e demandam discussao (a relacao e sempre muito de submissao e negacao de discussoes). E, por ultimo, o Japao e reconhecido como o lugar que as longas jornadas de trabalho 12-14 horas por dia sao bem vistas (nao import se isso leva a uma produtividade ou nao, se a pessoa esta sofrendo ou nao), o status valorizado aqui e quantas horas voce se mantem no ambiente de trabalho e anule a sua vida pessoal. Desse modo, a ciencia aqui, que demanda debate, discussao, opinioes e completamente negada pelo sistema hierarquico, bem como sao valorizados os estudantes que vao se degradando fisicamente ao longo do seu Doutorado. Adicionalmente, o Japao e um pais, extremamente xenofobico e, enquanto estudante internacional, esse preconceito e sentido em cada detalhe da vida academica, onde, nao importa o que voce faca, atinja ou demonstre: no final e cada esquina, voce sera sumariamente desacreditado, descredibilizado e desencorajado. E, toda essa situacao nao se aplica a mim, se estende a todos os outros estudantes internacionais que aqui convivo. E algo realmente muito grave e dificil de mudar.

Q16.text: A potencialidade da minha pesquisa ser muito menos explorada e ser fadada a menores alcances (achievements) ao considerar todo o abandono, a falta de interesse e o desapoio do meu Orientador de Doutorado (das coisas mais tristes e angustiantes que tenho enfrentado nesse Doutorado). Q26.text: First of all, in the Netherlands, bright people are leaving academia due to the lack of grants. It is very hard to pursue an academic career when you stay in the Netherlands. Therefore, I moved to the USA to follow working in academia as a postdoctoral researcher, and I hope that this experience will give me (some) advantage in grant applications when I move back to the Netherlands in 3-4 year.   Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. I think the Dutch system aims for a very high standard, which I like, but it diminishes opportunities to succeed later in your academic life.

Q26.text: Academia can be a great place to be - its a unique environment that can be relaxed and creative. Ultimately though, academia is geared towards giving power and a sense of entitlement to PIs, and has lost sight of its responsibilities regarding student wellbeing. Universities have given such power and status to PIs that they can't even control them anymore. PIs don't respect university/HR systems and standard work place etiquette.    A lovely example of academia failings: I collaborate with industry and have 1 university PI and 2 industrial PIs. I have had my industrial PI make inappropriate comments to me ranging from sexual harassment to being purely nasty. One example to give you a flavour: whats happened to your skin? how do you expect to be taken seriously when you look like a spotty teenager - you should really cover your spots up. I raised this with my uni PI and described other events that had made me uncomfortable and it was shrugged off as typical behaviour from this industrial PI. the take home message was basically that we gain funding and resource from the collaboration so leave it. At this point I had had a diagnosed breakdown after a very rough first year, so was in no position to argue. As a PhD student you sometimes forget that you're a person who is entitled to opinions and feelings.  Academia needs a huge shake up (a big old slap really!), from the top down.

Q26.original_text: I went into an area I didn't have very much previous experience in, molecular biology. I did this willingly, and my supervisor was well aware of this, but I was under the impression that the teaching would be more supportive than it has been. As such, catching up has been a much greater struggle than I felt it had to be, and this has changed my view of academia, and myself. Overall, I had the feeling that has been repeated by others when I've talked to them about this: beginner level information on a topic is usually freely available, but doesn't go into enough detail. Expert level information on a topic can usually be located, but is typically too dense to comprehend, particularly within the time-frame that you need to understand it. What you might call intermediate level information is usually lacking; you need most of the detail you would find in something aimed at experts but explained in a way that a beginner might have a shot at understanding readily. I have a degree in biomedical sciences, so I had some prior knolwedge of molecular biology. As such I found myself in the "intermediate" stage with too large a knowledge gap I needed to close in seemingly too short a time. I was expected to do end-point experiments within a week of starting that no one else had managed to make work, and with virtually no prior experience in the necessary tissue culture. My supervisor suggested I might have results in a fortnight. There were few relevant books I could get hold of - most were too simple anyway. There were few lectures available to go to, and although I tried to gain access to undergraduate and masters material in relevant areas, it took a long time before this access was granted, and even then, some of what would have been highly relevant was missing. You need a lot of valuable information to be very readily available if time frames are going to be that short and you are lacking prior experience. I do not feel, from communication with other graduate students, that I am particularly alone in this experience. It has been a struggle to get anyone to explain things in plain English, and frequently embarrassing to try. I have been told things like "I know this too well to explain it to you simply", which I personaly think is ridiculous but seems to be a generally accepted attitude in academica. Academic journals are no help in this department. While I appreciate the need for specialist terms in science, the more I eventually do understand, the more it appears that most of the language in journals is often pretty unneccessarily complicated. Sentences that could just be straight forward, even those that need specialist terms, are typically anything but. This makes comprehension that much harder. Q26.text: The academic system is designed to train PhD students to become PIs. In the process of doing so, PhD students gain valuable experience and transferable skills that make them competent and resourceful individuals. However, the expectation is very much that you would continue on to a post-doc position. This, in my view, is not a good thing given the relatively few academic jobs available. PhD programmes should establish closer links to industry and and other non-research related science careers to ensure that PhD students gain the skills aligned with these careers after they graduate, and build networks to facilitate job opportunities. PhD programmes and institutions also do not articulate well enough the capabilities of PhD graduates to employers in the wider sector, and can improve on this.  PIs and funding bodies have a lot of incentive to employ PhD students and post-docs in the short term on temporary contracts, but the academic system should incentivise instead the hiring of permanent staff scientists for those who want to be in the lab full-time. For those that don't, greater exposure to other career paths (eg. talks, networking opportunities, work experience placements and internships) is needed for PhD students' career progression.  In many cases, poor supervision from the PI and a negative group environment can detract from the PhD experience - this is really hard to judge from a short interview.

Q26.original_text: During my 7 years veterinary medical training in China, I got used to the “Chinese” schedule. We came to work at 8 AM and left around 10 PM, often working on the weekends. And forget about working on the weekend.  Because they don’t stay for those long hours like in China, I thought they don’t work hard enough. Later on I realized that I am actually the one who is not working hard. Staying in the lab/office longer than the others does not means I work harder. The other PhDs are all 100% focused on their work during the eight-hour working period and super organized, while I was taking so called “breaks (facebooking/instagramming/messing around here or there a bit)” . I struggled with my inefficient and poorly planned long working hours at the beginning, but finally resolved to change.  I don’t have to follow their working schedule, but I found that it is much more efficient, I am more engaged, and  I get to have a life after work for the first time.

Q26.text: The academic system needs a drastic overhaul. It has become a corrupt and abusive system. I would like to see major reforms at every single level. Most research is published for the sole reason of publishing a paper. Papers and impact factors have become the currency of academia; the desire to do Science for the sake of progress or humanity is largely non-existent. Most places and people care about the length of the CV, but no thought is spared towards the impact these studies may have had. Further, the Ph.D. student is left at the mercy of the supervisor and the academic system which tends to protect itself when questioned. Universities have become brands and they care too much about their brands. Harassment cases are quietly stamped out to protect the university's and the supervisor's reputation. This is true more so for international students who put their entire careers and lives on the line to work towards their Ph.D.s on a pittance. Lip service is paid to women empowerment, but women are consistently left out at every possible turn. A strong teaching effort is drummed up by universities, but everyone knows teaching takes away from one's ability to manufacture papers. It looks incredibly bleak for academia unless one is well-connected and comes with the right brand and backing. The way I see it, academia has stagnated and it does not look like things are changing for the better any time soon. Of course, one can write an entire article, and many have been written without much effect, about the publication system and the exorbitant cost of acquiring "knowledge" in today's world.

Q16.text: I find it absolutely baffling that academia, while propped up as the last bastion of ethical and moral purity, tolerates faculty and students with alarming behavioral issues. In my experience, I have seen faculty members get away with sexual harassment and abuse at multiple universities with supreme confidence. Further, the biggest lesson I have received during my Ph.D. is that academia rarely cares about merit or quality. There are, to the best of my knowledge, only two ways to get ahead: my advisor is well connected and/or I somehow manage to find my way onto a Nature or Science publication. Maybe this is to be expected given the shortage of jobs, but it makes academia an ideal breeding ground for abusive relationships. I also find that enough is not done to make incoming students understand how slim the chances of an academic career really are, post Ph.D. Maybe it is too much, and not even the point of a Ph.D., to train students for careers outside of academia. However, the system is nothing short of a scam if incoming students are, at the very least, not made aware of the reality of the job market. Precious few universities and departments actively expose their students to opportunities outside of academia by encouraging participation in workshops, conventions, presentations, alumni networks, etc. And no, it is not the sole responsibility of the incoming student to know how the job market is. It is similar to arguing that sweatshops employing immigrants in the Middle Eastern countries carry none of the blame and arguing instead that the blame must rest on the people working there "voluntarily".  And make no mistake, academia today is eerily similar to a sweatshop.

Q60.text: Yes! I entered my dissertation program focusing on research that bridges two different fields. In the beginning of my program, I was revered for that smart, forward-thinking twist to my research, and I was told repeatedly this is where the field needs to go (inter-disciplinary). Now, I am struggling to finish my dissertation, because every topic I suggest for my dissertation has been rejected by everyone in the department, since it is not traditionally within my field. And I never wanted this to happen to me, I had three options (I knew they were feasible, because another graduate student I worked with previously swiped one of those topics and graduated early and with praise) for dissertation topics as I entered the PhD program, because I knew I didn't want to be like other students I saw in my department that just appeared to take funding opportunities away from everyone while not progressing to graduation. Now I am that student. I even had a NSF DDIG proposal ready to submit (edits from the department lasted over 5 months, and it was ready!), and I was told they day of submission to our Office of Research, I should not submit, because no one in the department could supervise the project. I have since seen students AND professors independently come across those topics I have been steered away from, and those topics have been funded by major federal institutions, and the research yielded multiple publications in noteworthy journals. I am doing a dissertation project now that was not my idea, I have been handed the data, and it is my job just to analyze data that no one has used since the 1980's, just so I can graduate in 6 years. I know I sound like a complainer who is blaming everyone else for my problems. Maybe that is the case. I am saddened, because with those rejected topics have also gone my rose-colored glasses about the ability of research in academia to allow you to pursue passion projects. And even though my department publicly touts inter-disciplinary projects, there is no support for that in my department. It clearly took me too long for that to sink in.   Overall, I wish I had a mentor explain those hard facts to me; I wish I was smart enough to read between the lines to see inter-disciplinary research is not what my department produces; and I wish it did not have to be that way. Now, I just hope to graduate (later than I intended and with a project I am not sure contributes to modern society in any way), find an academic job (seemingly a one-in-a-million chance), and work to support inter-disciplinary research every day of my life.

Q26.text: Academic system is very bureaucratic and professors spend too much time in teaching and administrative duties. Since I like doing research, this discouraged me to pursue a professorship. This was a huge disappointment for me, because I thought I would have a strong and deep mentorship on research practice in the university setting.  The publish-or \-perish mentality is also a waste of the little time professors and postdocs have. This mentality makes people push for half-backed research results  (or hyped buzzwords) in order to increase publication count (or be present at a conference). The result (in my field at least) is a flood of low quality papers that are 90% written by students. This low quality takes enormous time from reviewers and makes conferences boring as participants barely ask questions or discuss the topics. Instead, I feel that most people are mostly interested in seeing and being seen.

Q26.text: I think the academic system is really powerful to develop professionally and personally. It is full of challenges that make you grow in all possible aspects. One can develope his/her own expertises over the years and built on them to participate in different projects and ideas. As a PhD student I can really see that I know much more now than when I started my degree (same way at that moment I knew more than before starting my Master's degree). The academic system is also very unique in the sense that it provides a multicultural environment where it is possible to meet and exchange ideas with people that come from all over the world. This leads to the formation of a very powerful scientific community. However, there are two things that I believe create a lot of issuess in the academic system as it is now. First, as I mentioned before, the only way to continue being in the system is by publishing and, of course, the higher the impact factor of the journal, the higher the chances to be successful and continue in academia. However, there are other factors apart from pure Science that affect a publication or the generation of the data and I think there should be a way to consider them. Second, there are very few (almost none) regulations on how to be a group leader. Even if PIs do get evaluated by the amount of publications that their group produce, nobody checks how they are treating their people and how they actually do Science. Once the position of group leader is reached, there is almost complete anarchy to do everything. This means that if you end up in a good group your possibilities to stay in the academic system will definetely improve. However, if you are in a group where the work environment/conditions are not the best, then it is highly likely that you don't want to do Science anymore after your PhD. And sadly, this is the reality of what is currently happening in academia and the amount of PhD students that want to pursue a career is dangerously decreasing because there is a high rate of group leaders that do not treat their people correctly.

Q26.text: In my opinion, the whole academic system has stopped on time. It is spent resources to graduate Doctors, yet after graduation, they spend more time grading, teaching, and apply for grants than actually doing research.  Hence, to free these high skilled workers, classrooms should be extinguished, and all courses should be online (class recorded with updates if any mistakes are identified), where students collaborate, but each learns at their own pace. The idea that it is not the quality of research, but the 'attractiveness' of the answer at the point of (attempted) publication, that ultimately defines the future success of PhD students is abhorrent. Q26.original_text: The academic system is mainly based on the assumption that you will continue with an academic career path once completing your PhD course. In my experience there is little guidance and support for those who have decided not to pursue that pathway.   The emphasis placed on publishing as many papers as possible, and the use of this as an indication of your research capability and work ethic creates a stressful environment where working excessively long hours is celebrated and encouraged. The "publish or perish" mentality has been the major challenge I have faced within the academic system as some areas/ disciplines in research are more time consuming than others, and thus the typical three year time period of a PhD program may allow some to publish numerous papers while others will be limited to a few, if any.       On the other hand, the academic environment allows for collaboration and I have found there is generally good working relationships between academic staff (although I acknowledge that my experience of this is only limited to two university environments). I have also found that there is an increasing emphasis placed on ensuring mental health within the academic system and there is growing support for PhD and graduate students. Q26.text: The academic system that we follow was set up with the right ethos. But in the execution we have all collectively faltered. It was one field of work which accommodated heterogeneity and diversity in all forms especially ideas and way of life but increasingly the system is trying to homogenize people making them loose their individuality. In older studies, journals reviewed and argued the science behind what the authors did, but now they review and make authors add more experiments which they want to see not necessarily needed for proving what the authors did. If big data is the current trend every research group is expected to have omics in their paper.  There is also this wave of applied research which as a standalone field is very good but inadvertently penetrates into basic research. All research cannot be applied immediately. Lots of drugs that are there in the market exist because their mechanism of action was a phenomenon some graduate student/post doc uncovered which could eventually get targeted. The original study may not even have proposed it. This also encourages researchers to portray hypothetical forced biomedical applications of their research findings and mislead people  when actually there may be none.  I also feel the system inherently assumes that people in academia don't have a life beyond work. They reinforce this assumption in their expectations from students and PIs. In fact its almost considered unusual if you are single and want to leave for home at decent hours after work. Family is the qualifier you need to enjoy time after work. This notion is largely in India. There are other inherent assumptions too like people doing science should look shabby and unkempt. This portrayal of scientists has become like a norm and if you don't fit into their mold you are not considered a serious scientist. People who are well dressed, especially women therefore have a hard time being taken seriously.

Q55.text: I wish I'd known that I could change departments when going from undergrad to grad studies. I thought since I did an undergraduate in biochemistry and I couldn't pursue a different graduate program. This limited the pool of PIs and projects I was looking into. I think this is probably common knowledge for many students but as my parents did no attend university, they had weren't able to guide me and prospective universities don't really advertise this.  I also wish I had known to look at the number of publications per year that my prospective PI was publishing. If there are very few, it could point to problems in the lab unless they are pursing lengthy studies (e.g. animal aging). Also are their postdocs in the lab? I now work in a lab with postdocs and having that extra mentoring is amazingly useful. I would now look for labs where the project I am placed on is ongoing and one-on-one mentoring/teaching is available - either from a postdoc or ideally, another graduate student who is passing the project on as they are about to graduate. My first project was leftover (and unpublished) from about 6 years before and hadn't been investigated since. This is a big problem because not only do you have no one to talk to but other labs could be close to publishing results that may make the previous work obsolete.

Q26.text: Garbage. While I've been lucky to have an excellent mentor and dedicated committee, the department and school I'm in offer at best little support for graduate students, and at worst, active attempts to sabotage those students. The default assumption is that a funded graduate student will teach all five years of their funding package, and the burden of responsibility of those teaching assignments has steadily increased over the five years of my PhD. For example, introductory lab teaching responsibilities have increased from 2 courses/week per TA to 3 courses/week per TA. This adds another 30 students' worth of grading to grading responsibilities, and another 5 hours per week between actual lab run time (3 hours), setup and cleanup (1 hour) and office hours (1 hour per lab session). This makes it impossible to confine teaching responsibilities to the 20 hours/week we're paid for (if you're spending 15 hours a week teaching, that leaves 5 hours a week to grade 90 lab reports. You try grading 90 lab reports in 5 hours. It doesn't happen--and that's not counting troubleshooting via email or addressing student concerns over email). Additionally, the number of trainings for teaching responsibilities we are expected to complete rises steadily every year, creating an unpredictable time commitment that varies from semester to semester. The end result is a burdensome, difficult to navigate system that means for most of the time you're working, you're doing teaching-related activities. Late in the programme, as I am, this can be deadly--you're faced with a choice of whether to assume debt for your last year or years or quit the programme due to simply not having time for research due to teaching responsibilities.  This wouldn't be so bad if those assignments were predictable and reliable, but they aren't. Colleagues haven't received their contract or their funding until well after the semester's actually started; I've been badgered for weeks by the financial services offices on campus because my tuition remission hasn't gone through in a timely manner. The actual wages do not reflect the cost of living. I am lucky because I receive a degree of financial support from my family, but medical and other kinds of debt among graduate students at my institution is common. I've been cycled through five separate teaching assignments before the semester started, with the administrators responsible indicating that I might not have one, even if my funding package guarantees it. Overall, it means there's a great deal of insecurity in funding even well into the programme and with a funding package.   There is no ability to unionize or organize for better working conditions. This university is in a right-to-work state, and the graduate student government, while claiming to be lobbying for better wages, is in effect toothless and has had no success in improving working conditions. With the expected ruling that graduate student workers are students first and workers second, there is little likelihood that this will change.
